# 2. The Sharing–Sparing Axis {#sec-sharing-sparing}

The axis answers one question about a site: **what happened to agricultural production on this ground?** Five positions, **S1** through **S5**, run from production continuing inside the array footprint to production ending on ground that was carrying a burden off-site. Every project on land occupies exactly one of them.

This is the second of the document's structural dimensions, and it is largely independent of [scale](1-the-scale-transect.qmd): a farmstead array and a regional complex can hold the same position. Scale says what a project is *able* to do before design begins; the sharing–sparing axis says what it did with the land.

**Why the question is critical.** Most public argument about solar on farmland is an argument about this axis, conducted without it. *We are losing farmland.* *It's dual use.* *That ground was never any good anyway.* *The lease is what keeps us farming.* Those are four claims about four different positions, and each of the terms in circulation — dual use, marginal land, farmland loss — smuggles in a position without naming one. Fix the position first and the rest of the conversation becomes possible: it settles what a project may fairly claim, what it still has to argue for, and which objections actually apply to it. A site's position is also the fact that survives a change of owner, offtaker, or seed mix, which is why it is worth recording precisely.

The framing is borrowed from conservation ecology's land-sharing / land-sparing debate, where the question of whether to farm gently everywhere or intensively in some places and not at all in others remains genuinely unsettled. The axis inherits that neutrality: it describes a real choice without ranking the options, and no position on it is better than another by definition.

### 2.1 The positions {#sec-positions}

::: {.position-table}
| Position | Description | Characteristic |
|---|---|---|
| **S1 — Full sharing** | Production continues within the array footprint, in the same ground | Vegetable [agrivoltaics](5-general-terminology.qmd#term-agrivoltaics); crops between rows |
| **S2 — Functional sharing** | Ground layer is productive but subordinate to the array; grazing, forage | Solar grazing at any scale |
| **S3 — Coexistence** | *Neither sharing nor sparing.* The array takes ordinary ground outright — production stops on it — and the revenue sustains the farm enterprise that holds it. The land and the farm coexist at the level of the business rather than the field | The lease that keeps a working farm solvent and in operation |
| **S4 — Idled-land sparing** | Array occupies ground already idle, marginal, or out of production, so that productive land is spared | Awkward remnants, fallow ground, brightfields |
| **S5 — Impaired-land retirement** | Production ends on ground that carried a measurable off-site burden — chronically low yields, high runoff, nutrient or pesticide export, irrigation draw beyond the aquifer's budget — or on ground positioned where that burden can be intercepted | Prairie strips on runoff-prone ground; retiring drainage-impaired irrigated fields |
:::

**The centre of the axis is coexistence (S3), and it is where most projects sit.** An ordinary array on ordinary ground produces no co-yield and retires no ground: that field becomes a power plant. What can still be restorative about it is the farm. Where the lease is the margin that keeps an operation from being sold — funding the succession, retiring the debt, carrying the farm through a bad decade — the project restores the enterprise even though it restores nothing in the soil. That is the [community & economic function](4-restorative-functions.qmd#sec-fn-community) (§4.5) doing its work, and it is why **S3 is the position where restoration is socioeconomic before it is biophysical**.

**S3 carries a threshold.** Coexistence is not simply "solar on farmland"; it requires that the arrangement sustain the farm enterprise holding the ground. Where the same conversion returns rent to a non-farming owner and the operation ends, the site is **bare conversion** — the identical ground fact without the restorative one. Bare conversion is the baseline the axis is read *against*, not a position on it. Which farm, and whose, is a real question rather than a rhetorical one: a lease can sustain a landowner and end a tenant's operation at the same time, so the test is applied to the actors set out in §4.5.

**The sparing wing splits on what the ground was doing beforehand.** S4 and S5 both end production, but they are different acts, and the difference is where the benefit lands. **S4** takes ground that had already stopped paying — the array goes to the awkward corner precisely so the good field is left alone — and the benefit accrues to *the land not taken*. **S5** ends production on ground that was exporting a burden, so it acts on *the ground taken itself*, and on the water leaving it. A flood-prone corner planted to solar spares the field next to it; a drainage-impaired field retired under prairie and panels stops sending nitrogen downstream. Both are removal; only one changes what the ground was doing to everyone else.

**A position records the ground fact, not the quality of the project.** Two S3 sites can differ completely — one carries gravel and herbicide, the other a native planting rich in pollinators — and they hold the same position because the same thing happened to production. What separates them is the [restorative functions](4-restorative-functions.qmd) layered on top. Ecological ground layers live there rather than on this axis: pollinator habitat, prairie, and native grassland are functions (§4) reachable from S2 through S5, so native grassland under a utility array is S3 carrying a biodiversity function, and the same planting on retired leaching ground is S5 carrying it. The axis says what happened to the production; §4 says what the land was made to do. Reading benefit straight off a position is the error §4 names as the [category correction](4-restorative-functions.qmd).

**Reading a site.** The positions are exclusive, and two questions in order settle which one applies.

1. **Does agricultural production continue within the footprint?** If it does, the site is **S1** (production in the same ground) or **S2** (a productive but subordinate ground layer) — whatever the ground used to be. A flood-prone corner that still carries the farm's sheep is S2, not S4.
2. **If production has stopped, what was the ground beforehand?** Ordinary productive land gives **S3**; ground already idle or marginal gives **S4**; ground carrying a measurable off-site burden gives **S5**. The same flood-prone corner, left to naturalize under the panels, is S4.

S3 asks one further question — whether the farm enterprise survives the conversion. Where it does not, the site is bare conversion rather than S3.

Two boundaries are worth stating plainly. **S4 holds unlike things together**: idled cropland, awkward remnants, reclaimed mine land, landfills, and brownfields share the one fact that the ground was already out of production, but differ in prior use, contamination, permitting path, remediation constraints on foundations and ground layer, and in what the community reads the reuse as meaning. The position records the shared fact; those differences belong to the site description. And **arrays on buildings hold no position at all** — a built surface has no prior land status because it occupies no land. That is the [A0 zero-land case](1-the-scale-transect.qmd#sec-zones) (§1.2), at the transect's origin. The axis is defined over ground; where there is no ground, there is no position.

### 2.2 Which positions scale allows {#sec-wedge}

The two dimensions are independent in principle but not fully in practice, and the constraint runs through [siting latitude](1-the-scale-transect.qmd#sec-siting-latitude) (§1.4) — the designer's freedom over which acres to occupy. A position is therefore not simply chosen: scale narrows the menu before the design meeting starts, and knowing which positions are realistically open at your scale is most of the value of reading the two dimensions together.

**Sparing requires the freedom to choose the ground.** Both sparing positions presuppose a designer who can select which acres to take. At A4–A5, where siting is governed by assembling contiguous land near a substation, that freedom is largely gone — a five-hundred-acre block contains good and poor ground mixed together. Large projects are pushed toward the S2–S3 middle by structural necessity rather than preference: if you cannot choose *which* ground, the remaining options are to do something worthwhile with all of it, or nothing with any of it.

**The two sparing positions behave differently at scale.** S4 thins for a geometric reason: idle remnants are *scattered*, so assembling a utility-scale project out of flood-prone corners is impractical where it is possible at all. S5 survives at scale wherever the impairment is *regional* rather than scattered — a drainage-impaired valley, a district over its groundwater budget. Where a whole landscape is impaired, retirement and scale stop fighting each other, because there is no cherry-picking to do. This is an expectation drawn from the archetypes rather than a measured result.

Read the axis from its centre: **S3 sits on the scale line**, with full and functional sharing (S1–S2) above it and the two removal positions (S4–S5) below. The feasible region is then not a rectangle but a **lens** — the *feasible wedge* — widest at A3 (Parcel) and closing toward the S2–S3 middle at both extremes of scale. It closes for different reasons at each end, and neither end is a hard wall.

![The feasible region as a lens on a centred five-position axis, widest at A3 (Parcel) and closing toward the S2–S3 middle at both extremes of scale. Grazing (S2) and coexistence (S3) run the spine at every scale. Solid points are exemplar practices; hollow points are exceptions that reopen a thinned corner. Hatching marks where the space thins — lightly at small scale (feasible but atypical or negligible), densely at large scale (strongly constrained).](../figures/fig_feasible_wedge.svg){#fig-wedge}

What to take from it:

- **Grazing and coexistence are the spine.** Functional sharing (S2) is genuinely available at every scale — a farmer's own flock at A1, a contracted vegetation-management service at A3, a multi-site rotation enterprise at A5 (§1.3). Coexistence (S3) is available at every scale for the opposite reason: it asks nothing of the ground. Everything else is more scale-conditional, which is why the lens narrows around these two at both ends.
- **Both extremes converge on the middle.** At A5 both wings narrow: siting is dictated by land assembly, so sparing loses the freedom to choose its ground, and tight budgets make full sharing's tall clearances and wide rows hard to justify. At A1 they narrow more gently — no one farms *under* a two-panel array, they farm next to it, and a spared idle corner is real but too small to affect land use.
- **The thinned corners are not walls.** Small-scale full sharing returns where the structure is purpose-built to farm under — greenhouse photovoltaics. Utility-scale full sharing returns with vertical bifacial arrays, whose open inter-rows relax the clearance constraint [@vaverkova2026]. Utility-scale S4 returns on uniformly low-value pre-disturbed land — reclaimed mine land, landfills, and brownfields ("brightfields") — where sparing and scale coexist without cherry-picking acres. Utility-scale S5 returns wherever impairment is regional, which is the exception with the most land behind it.
- **A3 (Parcel) is the widest part of the space.** All five positions are genuinely open at mid-scale, which is one reason Parcel-scale sites are disproportionately interesting as design exemplars.

*Native grassland is plotted at S3 because that is where it is most often built, not because it is a position; it is a [restorative function](4-restorative-functions.qmd) reachable across the axis, and at utility scale it carries documented biodiversity and soil-carbon gains [@walston2025; @krasner2025].*

**S1 is not equally attractive everywhere.** In-footprint crop benefit is strongly climate- and crop-conditional: pronounced in water-limited, high-radiation settings and for shade-tolerant crops [@barrongafford2019], but mixed to net-negative for staple grains and in temperate or humid settings, where shade costs yield without a compensating water saving [@weselek2019]. Full sharing is a regional proposition, not a universal one.

*The clearest counterexample to the reading above would be a utility-scale S4 project assembled from scattered marginal remnants on ordinary farmland, rather than from the uniform pre-disturbed ground the standing exception already allows. None is documented here, and one would be worth reporting.*

**Where the dual-use dispute sits.** American Farmland Trust holds that [dual use](5-general-terminology.qmd#term-agrivoltaics) requires active agricultural production sustained across the project's 30–40 year life, within the array footprint — structurally, a mandate for S1–S2. Critics argue that this marginalizes ecovoltaics, whose ecological ground layers deliver their value as a function rather than as production, and so sit at S3 and below. Stated as positions, the disagreement becomes tractable: it is a dispute about which stretch of the axis deserves the name, not about what the word means. This document describes that dispute rather than settling it. *(See §5, Agrivoltaics / Ecovoltaics.)*

### Associated Terminology

Terms this section introduces; cross-referenced terms link to their home section.

- **Sharing–Sparing Axis** — the second, scale-independent dimension: whether the array shares land with production, spares land by taking ground out of it, or neither. Five positions, centred on S3. Defined here.
- **S1 — Full sharing** — production continues within the array footprint, in the same ground.
- **S2 — Functional sharing** — ground layer is productive but subordinate to the array.
- **S3 — Coexistence** — neither sharing nor sparing: the array takes ordinary ground outright and the revenue sustains the farm enterprise holding it, so the restoration is socioeconomic rather than biophysical. The centre of the axis.
- **Bare conversion** — the same ground fact without the restorative one: ordinary ground converted, the operation ended. The non-restorative baseline the axis is read against, not a position on it.
- **Reading rule** — production first, then prior status: a site where production continues is S1–S2 whatever the ground used to be; only where it stops do S3–S5 apply, told apart by the ground's prior status.
- **S4 — Idled-land sparing** — array occupies ground already idle, marginal, or out of production, so productive land is spared.
- **S5 — Impaired-land retirement** — production ends on ground that carried a measurable off-site burden, or that sits where such a burden can be intercepted; the removal acts on the ground taken rather than on land elsewhere.
- **Feasible wedge** — the feasible region across scale and sharing, shaped like a lens: all five positions open at A3 (Parcel), closing toward the S2–S3 middle at both extremes — at A5 as land assembly and capital discipline remove the poles, at A1 as in-footprint farming and meaningful sparing both need more scale to be real. Grazing (S2) and coexistence (S3) are the spine; each thinned corner has an exception. Defined here (§2.2).
- **Siting latitude** — the designer's freedom over where the array goes; the constraint that makes the region a wedge. See [§1.4](1-the-scale-transect.qmd#sec-siting-latitude).
- **Agrivoltaics / Ecovoltaics** — production (S1–S2) versus ecological ground layers, which are functions (§4) reachable across S2–S5. See [§5](5-general-terminology.qmd#term-agrivoltaics).
